note: Standards and models that OHF field definitions draw on. Facts come from the version named in each entry. A licence of null means it is not established.

relations.field_basis: The catalogue paths listed take their concept from this standard. No term is copied.
relations.recommended_vocabulary: The catalogue names identifiers of this vocabulary for the paths listed. OHF does not bind or check the values.
relations.different_problem: The standard solves another task; OHF takes one idea from it for the paths listed.

standards.name: SEPIO Core Information Model
standards.version: sepio-linkml commit acb4ddde6011d6e0958048fb99e7d4aca057588f; many definitions are marked Draft and there is no release number
standards.scope: An information model for scientific assertions with their evidence and provenance, with separate proposition, statement, evidence line, data and contribution objects.
standards.difference: SEPIO is a general model of assertions and evidence. OHF takes from it the separation of proposition, statement, evidence line and contribution, and adds a card for one hypothesis with an author and an added zone, predictions and explicit gaps.

standards.name: Nanopublications
standards.version: Guidelines working draft; no numbered stable release
standards.scope: A small self-contained publication of one assertion with its provenance and publication information, in RDF named graphs.

license.value: Creative Commons ShareAlike Attribution 3.0 License, as stated in the footer of the guidelines document

standards.difference: OHF keeps the separation of assertion provenance from publication provenance. It binds the original artifact by SHA-256, not by a Trusty URI, and is a JSON card rather than RDF graphs.

standards.name: ICH E9(R1): estimands and sensitivity analysis in clinical trials
standards.scope: A regulatory guideline for specifying the treatment effect (estimand) a clinical trial targets: population, treatment, endpoint, intercurrent events and their strategies, and the summary measure.

license.value: ICH copyright; reuse under the conditions of the legal notice in the guideline
license.source: Legal notice, page 2 of the guideline PDF

standards.difference: OHF uses the estimand dimensions for the predictions of a hypothesis about an intervention. It does not require a biological hypothesis to be stated as a clinical trial, and applies a strategy for an intercurrent event only when the source states it.

standards.name: ARRIVE guidelines 2.0
standards.maintainer: Developed by Percie du Sert et al. with the NC3Rs
standards.scope: A reporting guideline for animal research: the Essential 10 and the Recommended Set of items an article should report.

license.source: permissions block of the article's full-text XML (Europe PMC, PMC7360023): Creative Commons CC0 public domain dedication

standards.difference: OHF uses ARRIVE items to describe the test system and study of a prediction or evidence line. For a hypothesis without its own experiment, a missing reporting item is not by itself a required gap.

standards.name: Micropublications
standards.maintainer: Developed by Tim Clark, Paolo Ciccarese and Carole Goble
standards.scope: An ontology that connects a scientific claim to its supporting data and methods and to its challenges, with explicit attribution.
standards.difference: OHF takes the idea of a representative claim among duplicates and of explicit assumptions. No Micropublications term is reused, because the licence is not established.

standards.name: CiTO, the Citation Typing Ontology
standards.maintainer: Developed by Silvio Peroni and David Shotton in the SPAR Ontologies project
standards.scope: Properties that state why one work cites another, such as citing as evidence, as a data source, or to dispute it.
standards.difference: CiTO types the relation between two works. OHF uses it only for the relation of a cited reference to the citing source; the direction of an evidence line toward a hypothesis is a separate OHF field.

standards.name: POPPER
standards.maintainer: Developed by Kexin Huang, Ying Jin, Ryan Li, Michael Y. Li, Emmanuel Candès and Jure Leskovec
standards.scope: An agent system that tests a hypothesis against supplied data by proposing testable consequences, running analyses and combining the results sequentially.
standards.difference: POPPER runs tests; OHF records a hypothesis. OHF takes from it the description of an intermediate test and its validity, and the falsification condition.

standards.name: OSF Preregistration
standards.scope: A form for specifying hypotheses, data collection and analysis before a study, including what the investigators already know of the data.
standards.difference: A preregistration plans one study. OHF links a prediction to such a plan and records what was known before the prediction, but does not itself plan a study.

standards.name: HyQue
standards.maintainer: Developed by Alison Callahan, Michel Dumontier and Nigam Shah
standards.scope: A system that evaluates formalised hypotheses, made of events joined by logical operators, against a knowledge base with explicit rules.
standards.difference: HyQue scores a hypothesis against a knowledge base. OHF takes from it the decomposition of a claim into atoms joined by AND, OR and XOR, and does not score.

standards.name: Evidence & Conclusion Ontology (ECO)
standards.scope: Terms for types of scientific evidence and for how an assertion was made, used to record the basis of annotations in biological databases.

license.source: Header of the released ontology file

standards.difference: ECO classifies the basis of an assertion; it does not state effect size or strength. The catalogue names ECO identifiers for evidence types; in OHF 1.0 the value is free text and is not checked against ECO.

standards.name: Biolink Model
standards.maintainer: Developed in the NCATS Biomedical Data Translator community
standards.scope: A data model and taxonomy of entities and associations for biological knowledge graphs, with predicates, qualifiers and knowledge-level and agent-type enumerations.

license.source: license key of the released model file

standards.difference: Biolink describes edges of a knowledge graph. OHF uses its predicates, context and knowledge-level and agent-type terms to describe a mechanism step and an evidence line; in OHF the values are free text.

standards.name: INDRA
standards.maintainer: Developed by Benjamin M. Gyori, John A. Bachman and collaborators
standards.scope: A JSON schema of molecular statements, such as activation or phosphorylation between agents, assembled into computational models.

license.source: Licence badge of the repository README

standards.difference: INDRA statements are machine-assembled molecular interactions. OHF describes a mechanism as entities and signed steps bound to a source, and keeps the hypothesis and negation flags of an evidence line.

standards.name: Hypothesis Evolution Protocol (HEP)
standards.version: arXiv:2607.09195v1, 10 July 2026; no code has been released
standards.maintainer: Izumi Takahara and Teruyasu Mizoguchi, Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo (authors of the paper)
standards.scope: An append-only, event-sourced registry and tool set that keeps each hypothesis of a language-model research agent as a persistent object: statement, elicited belief P(H), lifecycle state, provenance, predicted observable and lineage. It is evaluated on materials-science tasks.

license.source: licence link on the arXiv abstract page of v1

standards.difference: HEP keeps one self-reported belief per hypothesis inside one agent run, with five verdict states and four generation mechanisms. OHF takes the ideas of an elicited belief, a lifecycle state, the generation mechanisms de_novo, refine and merge, and lineage that excludes inspiration. In OHF 1.0 the lifecycle state is a label of the publisher; OHF defines no states and does not enforce transitions. It attaches confidence to attributed assertions with a declared scale and calibration, adds the origins import and published_restatement. HEP has no record versions; OHF record versioning is its own.

standards.name: MOOSE-Chem
standards.version: arXiv:2410.07076v6, 27 October 2025 (ICLR 2025); code at commit f8cda98a3bed30b0f0d85fba625e343d688461ab
standards.maintainer: Zonglin Yang and co-authors (Nanyang Technological University, Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and others); the code repository belongs to its first author
standards.scope: A language-model framework that composes chemistry hypotheses from a research background and one to three inspirations, usually papers, and ranks them. It builds on MOOSE (Findings of ACL 2024) and defines no record format.

license.source: licence link on the arXiv abstract page of v6; the code repository is MIT (LICENSE file at the pinned commit)

standards.difference: In MOOSE-Chem an inspiration is an input that a model retrieves and combines with the background to generate a hypothesis, and it must not be already known to relate to the background. OHF only records inspirations as attributed references in the provenance, and an inspiration does not make the hypothesis a descendant. OHF sets no count, novelty condition or retrieval step.

standards.name: Co-Scientist
standards.version: arXiv:2502.18864v2, 29 June 2026; Nature 655, 487–496 (2026), doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y. Version 1 of the preprint was titled "Towards an AI co-scientist"
standards.maintainer: Google Cloud AI Research, Google DeepMind and Google Research, with academic co-authors
standards.scope: A closed multi-agent system that generates, critiques, ranks and evolves research hypotheses and proposals from a research goal, applied to three biomedical problems. Its code and any record format are not public.

license.source: arXiv abstract page of v2 and the open-access statement of the Nature article; preprint v1 was posted under CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0

standards.difference: In the example proposal of Supplementary Note 10.2 a separate "Rationale and specificity" section follows the hypothesis. OHF takes only this idea of a separate, attributed rationale and keeps it in appendix.rationale, apart from structured fields. The sections are example output, not a published format.

standards.name: The AI Scientist
standards.version: arXiv:2408.06292v3, 1 September 2024; code at commit 1de1dbc1f4ee2c5f61e9c94348d55eb51d7fa2eb. The appendix.source_extensions example follows The AI Scientist-v2, arXiv:2504.08066v1
standards.maintainer: Sakana AI (licensor of the code repository)
standards.scope: A language-model pipeline that generates research ideas, runs experiments, writes a paper and reviews it automatically, shown on machine-learning research. It defines JSON shapes inside its prompts, not a data standard.

license.source: licence link on the arXiv abstract page of v3; the code at the pinned commit is under "The AI Scientist Source Code License", Version 1.0, which has no SPDX identifier

standards.difference: The AI Scientist writes limitations as free text in the generated paper and as a separate list from its automated reviewer; the idea records of version 2 have a "Risk Factors and Limitations" field. OHF keeps author-stated limitations apart from attributed curator commentary, and keeps sections of other formats as versioned extension records. Neither version defines an extension mechanism.

standards.name: The Unified Code for Units of Measure (UCUM)
standards.scope: A code system of unit symbols, prefixes and an expression syntax for unambiguous machine-to-machine communication of quantities with their units.

license.value: UCUM Copyright Notice and License, Version 1.1 (June 2024)
license.source: https://ucum.org/license; no SPDX identifier is stated

standards.difference: OHF recommends UCUM unit syntax but stores dose, duration, concentration and range values as strings that keep the source wording. It does not parse or validate UCUM expressions, and it adds what UCUM does not cover: administration basis, denominator, biological basis and time origin.
